name: 1969 March Storm

phenomena.details: Major geomagnetic storm on March 23-24 with Dst ~ −228 nT (WDC Kyoto) during the declining phase of Solar Cycle 20.

impacts.description: HF radio communications severely disrupted; polar radio routes experienced extended blackouts.
Aurora visible at mid-latitudes across North America and Europe; widely reported by the public.
GIC effects detected in long transmission lines and pipelines across North America.

papers.title: Threshold rigidity change during the magnetic storm of March 23-24, 1969
papers.authors: Wolfson, C. J., Nobles, R. A.
papers.keyFinding: Measured cosmic-ray cutoff-rigidity changes during the 23–24 March 1969 magnetic storm, documenting its magnetospheric intensity.

summary: The March 23-24, 1969 geomagnetic storm (Dst ~ −228 nT) was a notable event during the declining phase of Solar Cycle 20, causing HF radio blackouts and aurora at mid-latitudes, studied with early satellite-era instrumentation.
description: On March 23–24, 1969, during the declining phase of Solar Cycle 20, a major geomagnetic storm drove the Dst index to approximately −228 nT (WDC Kyoto final). The event occurred during the early satellite era when in-situ solar wind measurements were becoming available, providing a more complete picture of storm drivers than had been possible for earlier events. The storm caused significant HF radio disruptions, particularly on polar routes, and aurora was visible at mid-latitudes across North America and Europe. GIC effects were detected in power transmission infrastructure, though grid failures were not as severe as those that would occur in later, more infrastructure-dependent decades.
